title: Neonatal Skin Assessment
subtitle: Rashes, lesions, birthmarks in the newborn

root.label: Neonatal Skin Assessment
root.description: Rashes, lesions, birthmarks in the newborn

content.html:
Neonatal skin findings are extremely common — the vast majority are benign and transient. The challenge is distinguishing normal variants from pathologic conditions requiring evaluation. A systematic approach prevents both unnecessary workups and missed diagnoses.

Skin assessment framework:

  • Timing of onset (present at birth vs acquired)
  • Morphology (vesicles, pustules, papules, macules, patches, nodules)
  • Distribution (localized vs generalized, dermatomal)
  • Associated symptoms (fever, feeding difficulty, lethargy = systemic illness)
  • Maternal history (herpes, varicella, infections)

FeatureLikely BenignLikely Pathologic
TimingPresent at birth or first 48h, self-limitedProgressive, worsening, late-onset
Infant statusWell-appearing, feeding well, afebrileIll-appearing, febrile, poor feeding
MorphologyPapules, pustules with eosinophils (ETN)Vesicles on erythematous base (HSV), hemorrhagic, bullous
DistributionScattered, trunk predominantGrouped vesicles (HSV), generalized bullae (SSSS, EB)
Maternal hxUnremarkableHerpes, varicella, TORCH, STIs

Three critical questions for any neonatal skin finding:

  1. Could this be neonatal HSV? Any vesicle or cluster of vesicles in a neonate — especially on the scalp (monitor site), perioral, or grouped — must be evaluated for HSV until proven otherwise. START acyclovir empirically.
  2. Could this be a sign of systemic infection? Petechiae, purpura, diffuse pustules, or skin findings + fever/lethargy → sepsis workup.
  3. Does this birthmark need further evaluation? Large hemangiomas (PHACES), port-wine stain on V1 (Sturge-Weber), ≥6 café-au-lait macules (NF1), midline back lesions (spinal dysraphism).

The 'Big 5' benign transient neonatal skin conditions:

  • Erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN): Most common. Appears day 1–3. Erythematous macules/papules/pustules (1–3 mm) with surrounding flare, predominantly on trunk. Wright stain of pustule contents → eosinophils. Resolves spontaneously in 1–2 weeks. No treatment.
  • Transient neonatal pustular melanosis (TNPM): More common in dark-skinned infants. Present AT BIRTH (distinguishes from ETN). Superficial pustules on non-erythematous base that rupture easily leaving hyperpigmented macules with collarette of scale. Wright stain → neutrophils. Resolves; hyperpigmentation fades over months.
  • Milia: Tiny (1–2 mm) white/yellow papules on nose, cheeks, chin, forehead. Keratin-filled epidermal cysts. ~40–50% of newborns. Resolve spontaneously in weeks to months. Do NOT squeeze or extract.
  • Miliaria: "Heat rash" or "prickly heat." Caused by sweat duct obstruction. Miliaria crystallina (clear vesicles) = superficial; miliaria rubra (red papules) = deeper. Avoid overheating/overdressing. Resolves with cooling.
  • Neonatal acne (neonatal cephalic pustulosis): Small papules/pustules on face, usually weeks 2–4. Likely related to Malassezia colonization. Self-limited. Ketoconazole cream if severe. Resolves by 3–4 months.

ConditionOnsetMorphologyWright StainTreatment
ETNDay 1–3Papules/pustules + erythematous flare, trunkEosinophilsNone; resolves 1–2 wk
TNPMAt birthPustules on non-erythematous base → hyperpigmented maculesNeutrophilsNone; pigmentation fades months
MiliaAt birth1–2 mm white papules, faceN/ANone; resolves weeks
MiliariaVariableClear vesicles (crystallina) or red papules (rubra)N/ACooling; avoid overheating
Neonatal acneWeeks 2–4Papules/pustules on faceN/ASelf-limited; ketoconazole if severe
Sebaceous hyperplasiaAt birthTiny yellow papules on nose/upper lipN/ANone; resolves weeks
Harlequin color changeFirst daysSharply demarcated half-body redness (dependent side)N/ANone; transient, benign vasomotor

Parent counseling points:

  • "This is extremely common and will go away on its own."
  • "It is NOT an allergy, NOT contagious, and does NOT mean your baby is sick."
  • "No creams, ointments, or lotions are needed. Keep the skin clean and dry."
  • "Do not squeeze or pick at these spots."
  • "If your baby develops fever, poor feeding, or the rash looks different (blisters, spreading), bring them back immediately."

LesionTypeFeaturesEvaluation Needed?
Salmon patch (nevus simplex)Capillary malformationPink-red, flat, on nape ("stork bite"), eyelids, glabella ("angel kiss"). Blanches with pressure.❌ No — benign. Facial lesions fade; nape may persist.
Infantile hemangiomaVascular tumorAppears 1–4 weeks. Rapid proliferation (3–9 months), then slow involution (years). Superficial (red, "strawberry"), deep (blue, subcutaneous), or mixed.🟡 Refer if: periorbital (vision risk), airway (beard distribution), large facial (PHACES), hepatic, or ulcerating.
Port-wine stain (PWS)Capillary malformationPresent at birth. Dark red-purple, flat, does NOT fade. Grows proportionally with child. Darkens and thickens with age.🔴 V1 distribution → evaluate for Sturge-Weber (brain MRI, ophthalmology for glaucoma).
Kaposiform hemangioendotheliomaVascular tumorFirm, purplish, rapidly growing. Associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (consumptive coagulopathy).🔴 URGENT hematology/oncology referral.

LesionFeaturesSignificance
Dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots)Blue-gray macules/patches on sacrum, buttocks, back. More common in dark-skinned infants.BENIGN. Fade over years. DOCUMENT in chart to prevent confusion with bruising/abuse.
Café-au-lait maculesLight brown, flat, well-demarcated. 10–20% of normal newborns have 1–2.≥6 café-au-lait macules >0.5 cm in children → evaluate for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
Congenital melanocytic neviDark brown-black, raised, may have hair. Size varies.Giant CMN (>20 cm) → risk of melanoma (2–5% lifetime) and neurocutaneous melanosis. Derm referral.
Aplasia cutis congenitaWell-demarcated, absent skin (usually scalp vertex). May be ulcerated or scarred at birth.Usually isolated and benign. Large defects → evaluate for underlying skull defect. Associated with trisomy 13, Adams-Oliver syndrome.

Dermatology/specialist referral indications:

  • Infantile hemangioma: Periorbital (amblyopia risk), nasal tip ("Cyrano"), lip (feeding difficulty), beard distribution (airway hemangioma risk), large segmental facial (PHACES syndrome), hepatic, ulcerated, ≥5 cutaneous (hepatic screening US)
  • Port-wine stain V1 distribution: Ophthalmology (glaucoma) + brain MRI (Sturge-Weber leptomeningeal angiomatosis)
  • Giant CMN (>20 cm): Dermatology, brain MRI (neurocutaneous melanosis), long-term melanoma surveillance
  • Rapidly growing vascular tumor with coagulopathy: Kasabach-Merritt → hematology/oncology URGENT
  • ≥6 café-au-lait macules: Genetics evaluation for NF1
  • Midline lumbosacral lesions (dimple, tuft of hair, lipoma, hemangioma): spinal US (if <3 months) to rule out spinal dysraphism/tethered cord

Propranolol for Infantile Hemangiomas (AAP 2019 CPG):

  • Indication: Potentially disfiguring or functionally significant hemangiomas during proliferative phase (before 5 months old ideally)
  • Dose: Propranolol 1–3 mg/kg/day PO divided BID-TID
  • Initiation: Start low (1 mg/kg/day) and titrate over 1–2 weeks. Monitor HR and BP for 2 hours after first dose and dose increases.
  • Monitoring: HR, BP, blood glucose (risk of hypoglycemia — give with or after feeds). Watch for bronchospasm in infants with reactive airway.
  • Duration: Typically 6–12 months (through proliferative phase). Taper over 2 weeks when discontinuing.
  • Pre-treatment: Cardiac exam (murmur? → echo). ECG not routinely needed unless cardiac concern.
✓ Propranolol has revolutionized hemangioma management. Prior to 2008, treatment options were limited to steroids and surgery. Propranolol (Hemangeol) is now FDA-approved for infantile hemangiomas requiring systemic therapy.

content.html:
🚨 ANY vesicle in a neonate must be evaluated for HSV until proven otherwise. Start acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h EMPIRICALLY while awaiting PCR results. The cost of missing HSV is devastating.

HSV skin findings:

  • Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base — classic but not always present
  • Scalp (fetal monitor electrode site), perioral, conjunctival, anywhere
  • May appear as erosions/crusted lesions if vesicles have ruptured
  • Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells) is rapid but low sensitivity — PCR preferred
  • Send surface viral PCR swabs (mouth, nasopharynx, conjunctivae, rectum, vesicle base)

Staphylococcal skin infections:

ConditionFeaturesTreatment
Bullous impetigoFlaccid bullae with clear/cloudy fluid, often trunk/diaper area. S. aureus exfoliative toxin.Oral or IV antibiotics (nafcillin/oxacillin if MSSA; vancomycin if MRSA). Wound care.
SSSS (Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome)Generalized erythema → superficial desquamation. Positive Nikolsky sign (skin separates with gentle pressure). Exfoliative toxin-mediated (NOT infection of skin itself).IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics. Gentle skin care. Fluid/electrolyte management. Cleavage plane is superficial (within epidermis) — better prognosis than TEN.
Skin abscessFluctuant, erythematous, tender noduleIncision and drainage. Culture. Antibiotics if surrounding cellulitis or systemic signs.

Omphalitis (umbilical infection):

  • Erythema, induration, and/or purulent discharge from the umbilical stump
  • Can progress RAPIDLY to necrotizing fasciitis, peritonitis, portal vein thrombosis, sepsis
  • Organisms: S. aureus, Group A strep, E. coli, polymicrobial (including anaerobes)
  • Treatment: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin + gentamicin ± metronidazole). Surgical debridement if necrotizing fasciitis.
  • When to worry: Periumbilical cellulitis extending >2 cm, dusky/necrotic skin, systemic signs (fever, poor feeding, tachycardia), crepitus
🚨 Omphalitis can be rapidly fatal. Any periumbilical erythema with discharge or systemic signs = start IV antibiotics immediately and consider surgical consultation for possible necrotizing fasciitis.

Congenital syphilis skin findings:

  • Maculopapular rash (copper-colored), especially palms and soles
  • Condylomata lata (moist, flat, gray-white lesions at mucocutaneous junctions)
  • Desquamation/peeling of palms and soles
  • Rhinitis ("snuffles") — bloody/purulent nasal discharge
  • Highly infectious — contact precautions until treated
  • Treatment: IV penicillin G × 10 days (see infectious disease tree)

Congenital candidiasis:

  • Generalized erythematous papulopustular rash at birth or within first 24 hours
  • Unlike diaper candidiasis (which is localized); congenital involves trunk, extremities, face
  • Risk: preterm + chorioamnionitis + foreign body (cerclage)
  • In preterm: can progress to invasive candidiasis — treat aggressively with systemic antifungals

Preterm skin physiology:

  • The stratum corneum (outermost skin barrier) is thin and immature in preterm infants, especially <30 weeks
  • At 24 weeks: stratum corneum is essentially absent → massive transepidermal water loss (TEWL), high risk of infection, percutaneous drug/toxin absorption
  • Skin maturation occurs over 2–4 weeks postnatally regardless of GA (epidermal barrier function approaches term by 2–3 weeks in most preterm infants)
  • Until maturation: TEWL can be 10–15× that of term infants → significant fluid and caloric losses

Six evidence-based skin care practices for preterm infants:

  1. Humidity: 80–90% relative humidity in incubator for first 7–14 days for infants <28 weeks. Wean gradually. Reduces TEWL by 50%.
  2. Minimize bathing: No full immersion bath until umbilical cord separates and infant is stable. Spot-clean with warm water only. Avoid soap in first 2 weeks. When bathing, use pH-neutral (5.5) liquid cleanser.
  3. Emollient use: Sunflower seed oil or medical-grade emollient may improve barrier function. Apply sparingly. Avoid petroleum-based products in ELBW (infection concern — mixed evidence). Coconut oil has antimicrobial properties (promising but limited neonatal data).
  4. Adhesive management: Use silicone-based adhesives (Mepitac, silicone tape). Remove adhesives with silicone-based remover. NEVER use alcohol-based adhesive removers on preterm skin. Minimize tape use — use hydrocolloid barriers under adhesives.
  5. Chlorhexidine caution: For skin antisepsis in infants ≥26 weeks. In infants <26 weeks: risk of chemical burns — use with extreme caution, brief contact time, pat dry immediately. Some units avoid chlorhexidine entirely in <26 wk and use sterile saline or povidone-iodine instead.
  6. Minimize skin breakdown: Position changes q2–4h with gel mattress or sheepskin. Transparent film dressings over bony prominences. Keep diaper area clean and dry with barrier cream (zinc oxide). Monitor for pressure injuries — even NICU patients develop them.

Adhesive-related skin injury prevention:

  • Medical adhesive-related skin injury (MARSI) occurs in up to 17% of NICU patients
  • Use pectin-based or hydrocolloid barriers under ALL adhesives (tape, ECG electrodes, pulse ox probes)
  • Use silicone-based tapes preferentially (less adhesion to epidermis)
  • Allow adhesives to "cure" before applying to skin (reduces adhesion force)
  • Remove adhesives by pulling parallel to skin surface (NOT perpendicular) while supporting underlying skin
  • Use silicone-based adhesive remover (e.g., Cavilon No Sting Barrier Film, Niltac) for stubborn adhesives
  • NEVER forcibly remove adhesives from preterm skin — this can remove the entire epidermis

Petechiae/purpura in a neonate — differential:

CauseAssociated FeaturesWorkup
ThrombocytopeniaNAIT, TORCH, sepsis, DICCBC, plt count, maternal plts, TORCH screen
CoagulopathyDIC (sepsis, asphyxia), VKDBPT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, vitamin K hx
InfectionSepsis (bacterial, viral), TORCHBlood cx, CRP, TORCH workup
Birth traumaFacial petechiae from cord around neck or vertex presentationClinical diagnosis — benign, resolves in days
Child abusePattern does not match birth trauma; suspicious historyFull evaluation per child protection protocol
⚠️ Petechiae limited to the face and upper trunk after vertex delivery or tight nuchal cord = common and benign. Petechiae below the nipple line or generalized = concerning and requires full workup.

"Blueberry muffin" rash: Blue-red papulonodules from dermal extramedullary hematopoiesis. Indicates the bone marrow is failing and red cell production is happening in the skin.

  • TORCH infections: CMV (#1), rubella, toxoplasmosis, syphilis
  • Hematologic: Rh hemolytic disease (severe), congenital leukemia, TAM (trisomy 21), neuroblastoma (metastatic)
  • Workup: CBC with diff and smear (blasts?), TORCH screen, abdominal US (hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal mass), bone marrow aspirate if hematologic malignancy suspected

Collodion baby:

  • Born encased in a tight, shiny, translucent membrane (collodion membrane)
  • Membrane cracks and peels within first 2 weeks
  • Most commonly: lamellar ichthyosis or congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma
  • ~10% are "self-healing" collodion babies (membrane peels and skin underneath is normal)
  • Acute management: Humidified incubator (high humidity essential — massive TEWL), emollients, monitor for fluid/electrolyte losses, temperature instability, infection risk (broken barrier). May need NICU admission.
  • Ectropion (outturned eyelids) and eclabium (outturned lips) — ophthalmology consult, eye lubrication

Harlequin ichthyosis:

  • Most severe form of ichthyosis. AR (ABCA12 gene mutation).
  • Thick, plate-like armor of skin with deep fissures at birth. Severe ectropion, eclabium.
  • Previously uniformly fatal; now improved survival (~50%) with intensive NICU care and retinoids
  • Management: humidified incubator, emollients, systemic retinoids (acitretin), ophthalmology, plastic surgery consult, infection prevention, nutrition support
